note.text:
The same method works when there are radicals (groups of atoms) or several products.
Tips:
• Balance metals first, then non-metals, and leave hydrogen and oxygen to the end.
• A radical that stays the same on both sides (SO₄, CO₃, NO₃, OH) can be counted as one unit.
• Check every element at the end.
Examples:
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ (two Cl and two H on each side).
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (C: one; H: four; O: four on each side).
2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ (K: two; Cl: two; O: six on each side).

steps: Carbon is balanced ({1} each side). Hydrogen: {4} on the left, so put {2} in front of H₂O.
Oxygen on the right is now {2} + {2} = {4}, so put {2} in front of O₂.

cards.idea: Balance metals first, then non-metals; leave hydrogen and oxygen to the end.
example: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂: zinc is already equal.

cards.idea: Count every element on both sides at the end, including the oxygen in every formula.
example: O: four on the left; two in CO₂ and two in {2}H₂O.

check.prompt: How many {nameOf(e)} atoms are on the right side of {eqStr(i)}?

misconceptions.explain: Multiply by the big number in front of each formula too.

solution: Multiply the small number after {e} by the big number in front of each formula.
Add them for the right side: {answer}.

cards.idea: A balanced equation keeps the correct formulae; only the numbers in front change.

misconceptions.explain: Count the atoms: they are not equal on both sides yet.
Too many: count that element again on both sides.

solution: Count each element on both sides.
Only {answer} has equal numbers of every atom.

misconceptions.explain: With one, the atoms are not equal on both sides: count again.

solution: Count each element on both sides.
The number that makes them equal is {answer}.
